newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada, veteran peacekeeper, offers neutral venue.
newsitem.headline: Canada, veteran peacekeeper, offers neutral venue.

text.p: When the Japanese and Peruvian leaders sit down for talks on the Lima hostage crisis on Saturday in Canada, they will do so with the aid of one of the world's most experienced peacekeeping nations.
Since the Suez crisis of the 1950s, Canada has a long if slightly tarnished history of playing the role of the world's honest broker.

"We are seen as the Scandinavians of the North Atlantic," said Janice Stein, a political science professor at the University of Toronto. "And it's generally consistent with our high reputation in the world."

Political analysts believe Canada was chosen as the venue for the summit as a result of a combination of convenient geography for the two leaders and for Canada's early role in helping to mediate in the crisis.
Leftist Tupac Amaru rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence on Dec. 17 and took more than 500 residents hostage. All but 72 have been released.

Canada's ambassador to Lima, Anthony Vincent, was among those orginally held hostage but was released with three other diplomats and charged with helping to mediate between the Peruvian government and the rebels.

Vincent, a British-born career diplomat for Canada, is known in diplomatic circles for his cool reserve under fire as well as his long experience, including a stint as head of Canada's international counterterrorism branch between 1988 and 1992.

Vincent will play facilitator in the talks between Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, and will have some political collateral to use with the two delegations seeking possible solutions in the crisis.
"Our role and his is best described as facilitator," said a Canadian foreign ministry official. "Vincent certainly has considerable experience with the whole situation."
Jim Hanson, executive director of the Canadian Institute of Strategic Studies in Toronto, said Canada's role in the world would be enhanced by the summit. "It's quite a feather in our caps," he said.

Canada boasts a proud diplomatic tradition in world affairs that dates back to Suez Crisis in 1956, when its foreign minister of the day, Lester Pearson, won a Nobel prize for his plan to use a peacekeeping force to ease the French and British out of Egypt.

Canada has joined virtually every major peacekeeping mission launched by the United Nations and the country takes no small amount of pride in its role as a moderate power with a voice on the world stage.

Recently, however, there has been one serious blot on that record. It was with deep shame that Canadians awoke to headlines and newscasts revealing Canadian paratroopers from an elite regiment tortured and killed a 16-year old youth during a UN peacekeeping mission to Somalia in 1993.

A commission of inquiry was set up to investigate the incident, which has become known in Canada as "the Somalia affair" and the government's reaction. That commission has been told by the government to conclude its work by March.
